title: The LORD Answers from the Whirlwind
summary: At last God speaks. Out of the whirlwind the LORD confronts Job with questions: where was he when the earth's foundations were laid, who shut in the sea, has he commanded the morning, walked the depths, seen the gates of death, entered the storehouses of snow, bound the stars, or sent the lightning. The speech moves from the founding of the world through the sea, light, weather, and heavens, and ends with God feeding the lion and the raven.
story: This is the moment the whole book has been waiting for. Job has demanded a hearing again and again, most recently in his final oath, where he signed his defense and asked the Almighty to answer him (31:35). The friends and Elihu have spoken for God; now God speaks for himself. For the first time since the prologue, the narrator uses the covenant name, the LORD, for the speaker. Yet God doesn't answer the question Job asked. He never mentions the heavenly test of chapters 1 and 2, never charges Job with the sins the friends alleged, and never explains the suffering. Instead he takes Job on a tour of creation. The first speech runs through chapter 39; Job's brief reply comes in 40:3-5, followed by a second speech about Behemoth and Leviathan.
historical:
The speeches from the whirlwind share the book's patriarchal setting and cannot be tied to a datable event. Their picture of the world, though, is drawn from the shared cosmology of the ancient Near East. The earth is imagined as a building with foundations, measurements, and a cornerstone (verses 4 to 6). The sea is a force that must be confined behind bars and doors (verses 8 to 11). There are storehouses of snow and hail (verse 22) and gates of death beneath the earth (verse 17). Neighboring cultures used similar images, often in stories of gods battling the sea to create order.

The constellations named in verses 31 and 32 were known across the ancient world. The Hebrew kimah is usually identified with the Pleiades and kesil with Orion (kesil means fool, and some think it reflects a legend of a giant bound in the sky). The Bear and her cubs is a less certain identification, and some translators render it as another star group. The term mazzaroth in verse 32, translated constellations, is found only here and its exact meaning is debated; suggestions include the signs of the zodiac or a particular star or planet.
cultural:
Two features of the speech would have struck an ancient reader. The first is its courtroom setting turned inside out. Job had wanted to question God as a plaintiff questions a defendant; now God tells Job to brace himself like a man (literally, gird up your loins, tucking the long robe into the belt for hard work or combat) and to answer as the one questioned. The reversal is not cruel but clarifying: Job had spoken as though he could see the whole case.

The second is what God chooses to talk about. Much of the chapter concerns places humans never go and things that serve no human purpose: rain on a desert where no man lives (verse 26), the deep sea, the realm of the dead, the hunting of lions, the feeding of ravens. Ancient Near Eastern thought often pictured the world as ordered for the service of the gods or for human use. God's speech describes a world far larger than human interests, full of things he tends simply because he made them. The raven, an unclean bird under Israel's later law, is still fed by God when its young cry out to him.
literary: The speech is a sustained sequence of questions, most of them rhetorical, delivered in some of the finest Hebrew poetry in the Bible. It opens with a challenge (verses 2 and 3), then moves in a rough order through the cosmos: the founding of the earth (verses 4 to 7), the sea (8 to 11), morning and dawn (12 to 15), the depths and the underworld (16 to 18), light and darkness (19 to 21), snow, hail, lightning, and rain (22 to 30), the stars (31 to 33), clouds and wisdom (34 to 38), and finally the animals, beginning with the lion and the raven (39 to 41). Irony runs through it; in verse 21 God says, in effect, surely you know, since you were already born then. The images are vivid and often tender: the stars singing at creation, the sea wrapped in swaddling clothes like a newborn, the dew and frost given birth.

outline.t: The LORD speaks from the whirlwind
The sea shut in behind doors
The depths, death, light, and darkness
Snow, hail, lightning, rain, and ice
The stars, the clouds, and wisdom
Food for the lion and the raven

doctrines.note: God laid the earth's foundations, set the sea's boundaries, and brings rain, frost, and dew. The chapter is one of the Bible's great creation texts, presenting the world as God's carefully built and continually tended work.
God doesn't only make the world; he sustains it daily, sending rain where no one lives and feeding the lion and the raven. His care reaches far beyond what humans see or need.
God asks who put wisdom in the heart and who has the wisdom to count the clouds. True wisdom begins with recognizing the limits of human understanding before the Creator's.
God answers Job in person. Even without explaining the reasons for Job's suffering, his speaking is itself the answer Job most needed: God has not abandoned him and has not been silent.

words.note: Searah, whirlwind or tempest. The storm is a frequent setting for God's appearing in the Old Testament; Elijah was taken up in one (2 Kings 2:11, the same word). Here the whirlwind is both overwhelming and personal: from it God speaks to one man by name.

Etsah, counsel, plan, or design. God's first question accuses Job of obscuring his counsel by words without knowledge. The word points to God's purposes in governing the world. Job's error was not asking questions but speaking as though he understood God's design.

Yasad, to found or lay a foundation. The verb in verse 4 pictures God as a master builder laying the earth's foundation, and the following verses fill in the builder's work: measurements, measuring line, footings, and cornerstone.

Kimah, usually identified as the Pleiades, the cluster of stars in the constellation Taurus. It appears also in Job 9:9 and Amos 5:8, both times with Orion. God asks whether Job can bind its chains, pointing to his rule over the heavens as well as the earth.

christ: The New Testament identifies the one through whom God founded the world. John says of the Word that all things were made through him (John 1:3), and Paul says of Christ that in him all things were created and in him all things hold together (Colossians 1:16-17). The questions God asks Job, about who laid the cornerstone and who feeds the ravens, are answered in the gospel by pointing to the Son. Jesus himself used God's care for the ravens to teach his disciples not to be anxious (Luke 12:24). And the God who answers Job from the storm is later seen in a man who stills the storm with a word. These links are drawn by the New Testament, not hidden in Job; they show that the Creator who confronts Job is the same God who comes near in Christ.

hard.q: Why doesn't God explain Job's suffering? Isn't this speech simply overpowering him?
hard.a:
Many readers feel this. Job asked why he was suffering, and God answers with questions about the stars and the sea. Some critics have read the speech as a display of raw power that silences Job without answering him. Others, reading the book as a whole, see several things happening. First, the speech isn't hostile: God comes, speaks personally, and talks about his tender care for creatures no one else notices. Second, it corrects the premise that both Job and his friends shared, that the world runs by a simple rule of reward and punishment that humans can inspect; the world God describes is vast, wild, and ordered by a wisdom beyond human sight. Third, in the epilogue God says Job has spoken rightly of him, which suggests the speech is not a condemnation.

The book never says the reasons for suffering are unknowable in principle. It shows that Job didn't know them, that God did, and that meeting God proved enough for Job even without the explanation. Readers who want a theory of suffering from this chapter won't find one; they will find a God who shows up.

questions: God asks Job, “Where were you when I laid the foundations of the earth?” How does that question change the way you hold your own questions about suffering?
God describes rain falling where no one lives and food for ravens. What does that tell you about how God values parts of creation that seem useless to us?
Job wanted an explanation and received an encounter. When have you needed God's presence more than you needed an answer?
